title: Checkpoint: Every Risk Needs a Written Owner, a Funded Backstop and a Record
summary: This checkpoint pulls the contracts, insurance, risk, disputes, records and audit phase into one chain. A risk is allocated by the contract, transferred by insurance or surety, owned in the register, proved by the record and tested by an independent reviewer. A break anywhere in the chain sends the loss back to the owner.
body:
Every risk on a project ends up with somebody. The whole of this phase is about making sure that somebody is chosen in writing, can actually pay, and can be proved to have agreed, before the loss arrives rather than after.

Recall

Q. What does an independent reviewer, such as a lender's monitor or a quantity surveyor auditing cost, add that your own team cannot?

A. A view from someone who did not make the decisions being checked and has no stake in them looking good. The value is the independence; a reviewer chosen and briefed to agree adds nothing.

Q. What makes a record contemporaneous, and why does it matter?

A. It was made at the time of the event, by someone who saw it, and has not been edited since. In a dispute, a record made at the time is far more persuasive than a recollection assembled later.

Q. What is a BATNA?

A. Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what you will actually do if this deal fails. It sets the point below which you should walk away.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer is the one party on a project who cannot pass every risk on. Lenders lend against your equity, contractors price what they accept, insurers cover what the policy words cover, and whatever falls between them falls on you. This phase taught the six tools that decide where a loss lands. The checkpoint asks whether you can use them as one system rather than six subjects.

The chain of six links

In plain English: before anything goes wrong, you decide who pays, you make sure they can pay, you keep track of what is left, and you keep the proof.

The professional framing is a chain with six links. One, allocation: the contract says which party bears a risk, through indemnities, limitation of liability, exclusions of consequential loss, unforeseen ground clauses, force majeure and liquidated damages. Two, transfer: insurance and surety put money behind the allocation, through builder's risk, liability cover, professional indemnity, bonds and letters of credit. Three, retention: the risk register owns whatever is left, with an owner, a trigger and a contingency for each item. Four, resolution: the dispute ladder settles what the paper did not settle clearly. Five, proof: records show what was agreed and what happened. Six, challenge: independent review tests whether the other five links are real.

Each link depends on the one before it. An indemnity from a contractor with no insurance and no assets is an allocation with nothing behind it. A perfect policy is worthless if the notice clause was missed and nobody can prove when the event occurred. A register that lists a risk the contract already gave to the contractor wastes contingency; a register that misses a risk the contract gave back to you hides it.

Worked example, hypothetical numbers. A site meets unexpected rock costing 1,000,000 dollars to remove. Under contract A, the contractor accepted ground risk with no relief: the contractor pays, if it is solvent. Under contract B, an unforeseen ground clause gives the contractor relief for conditions a competent contractor could not reasonably have foreseen from the site information provided: you pay, unless you can show the rock was in the geotechnical report. Under contract C, the parties agreed a baseline geotechnical report: the contractor carries conditions up to the baseline and you carry everything worse. The same rock, three owners, decided entirely by words signed months earlier. Your register should show the 1,000,000 dollars only where the contract left it with you.

Say that out loud now.

A backstop must be funded

In plain English: a promise to pay is only as good as the money behind it.

Professionally, you check every allocation for a backstop. A cap on liability tells you the most you can recover. A bond or letter of credit tells you who pays if the promisor cannot. An insurance policy tells you which events are covered and which are excluded, and the policy words, not the broker's summary, decide. A waiver of subrogation means an insurer that pays a claim cannot then sue the other insured parties; it keeps the project parties from suing each other through their insurers, but you must check every policy carries it consistently.

Second worked example, hypothetical. A contract sets liquidated damages for delay at 10,000 dollars a day, capped at 10 percent of a 20,000,000-dollar contract sum, which is 2,000,000 dollars. Your own cost of delay, interest, lost rent and extended overheads, is 25,000 dollars a day. After 200 days the cap is reached: 200 days at 10,000 is 2,000,000. Every day after that costs you 25,000 dollars with nothing coming back. If the realistic delay case in your risk register is 300 days, you have 100 uncovered days at 25,000, or 2,500,000 dollars, plus the 15,000-dollar daily gap over the first 200 days, 3,000,000 dollars. Uncovered exposure: 5,500,000 dollars. The liquidated damages clause did not remove the delay risk; it priced a slice of it. The rate and cap are commercial terms, negotiated deal by deal, not a standard.

Proof and challenge close the chain

In plain English: a right you cannot prove, or a plan nobody has tested, is a hope.

The last two links are the ones owners skip because they feel like paperwork. The record proves which allocation applies: when the rock was found, what the geotechnical report said, when notice was given and to whom. Independent review asks whether the other links are real: whether the contractor's bond is current, whether the policies match the contract's insurance requirements, whether the register's severe cases are honest. A peer reviewer, a lender's monitor, a quantity surveyor auditing cost, or a commissioning authority each tests one part of the system. None of them tests all of it unless you brief them to.

Applied to the rock example: under contract C, the owner's whole position depends on showing the rock was worse than the baseline. That depends on survey records made when the rock was exposed, signed by both sides, before it was removed. Once the rock is gone, the evidence is gone with it. The chain is only as strong as the day-one record.

How the best do it

Large, disciplined contractors run a formal review before they sign a major contract: a team that was not involved in pricing reads the contract, the risk register and the insurance programme together and asks one question of every risk, who holds it and what pays for it. A small developer can copy that in one afternoon. Before signing, put the contract's risk clauses, the insurance summary and the register on one table, one row per risk, and leave no row without a named holder and a named source of money.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: insurance proceeds, liquidated damages and settlement payments may be treated differently for tax; ask before you sign how each will be characterised. Liability: every gap in the chain becomes the owner's liability, and through any guarantee, possibly yours personally. Banking: lenders read the insurance programme and bonds as part of their security and will require them in the loan conditions. Governance: decide in writing who may give and receive contractual notices, and who may settle a claim. Estate: claims and limitation periods can outlive a project; your records must survive you. Exit: a buyer will ask for warranties, latent defect cover and open claims, so an unresolved chain lowers the price.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on the contract allocation; insurance broker, on the programme; quantity surveyor, on the priced risk register.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming a risk has gone because a clause mentions it. Clauses allocate; they do not pay. The control is the one-table review above, repeated at signing, at each major change and at substantial completion.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the contract, the policies and the register on different days with different advisers, so nobody sees that the three documents disagree. Read them together, in one sitting, against the same list of risks.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught stress tests: base, downside and severe cases, and the triggers that move you between them. The delay example today is a stress test applied to a contract clause. A liquidated damages cap is a break-even you can calculate, and the day the cap is reached belongs in your downside case.

Recap

Risk moves through six links: allocation, transfer, retention, resolution, proof and challenge. Each link needs the one before it, and every allocation needs funded money behind it. Read the contract, insurance and register together, and price what is left.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: Grenfell Tower and the certificates nobody tested.
checklist: I read the contract, the insurance programme and the risk register together, in one sitting.
Every risk on my list has a named holder and a named source of money.
I know the cap on every liability and liquidated damages clause and the day it is reached.
I check that every policy carries a consistent waiver of subrogation.
I hold a written list of who may give and receive contractual notices.
My register carries only the risks the contract leaves with me.
I repeat the one-table review at signing, at major changes and at completion.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every risk on a project ends up with somebody, and this whole phase is about choosing that somebody in writing before the loss arrives. Think of six links. The contract allocates the risk. Insurance and surety put money behind the allocation. The risk register owns whatever is left, with an owner and a contingency. The dispute ladder settles what the paper left unclear. Records prove what was agreed and what happened. Independent review tests whether the other links are real. Each link needs the one before it. An indemnity from a contractor with no money is a promise with nothing behind it. A liquidated damages clause does not remove delay risk; it prices a slice of it up to a cap, and every day past the cap is mine. So before I sign, I put the contract, the policies and the register on one table, and no risk leaves that table without a named holder and a named source of money.
terms: Allocation — the contract's choice of which party bears a given risk, through clauses such as indemnities, caps and unforeseen ground provisions.
Backstop — the money that stands behind an allocation, such as insurance, a bond or a letter of credit, if the promising party cannot pay.
Baseline geotechnical report — an agreed description of expected ground conditions; the contractor carries conditions up to it and the owner carries conditions worse than it.

hostile.q: Your contractor has accepted ground risk. Why is it still in your risk register?
hostile.a: Because acceptance is only as good as the contractor's ability to pay. The register holds the residual: the chance the contractor fails, disputes the clause, or claims the conditions were unforeseeable from the information we provided. I carry a smaller contingency against that, sized to the contractor's balance sheet and bond, not the full cost of the risk.

title: Grenfell Tower 2017: The Certificates Nobody Tested
summary: Grenfell Tower in London burned on 14 June 2017 and 72 people died. The public inquiry's final report in 2024 described a long chain of failures in which manufacturers, consultants, contractors, building control and government each relied on someone else's assurance. The lesson for an owner is that a certificate is a claim to be checked, not a risk transferred.
body:
At Grenfell Tower, almost every party could point to a document that told them the building was safe. The tragedy was that no one in the chain owned the question of whether those documents were true.

Recall

Q. What is a red team in a project review?

A. A group deliberately asked to attack a plan, structure or estimate, looking for how it fails, rather than to confirm it.

Q. Why should records be kept even after a project is handed over?

A. Because claims, latent defects and investigations can arise years later, and the record made at the time is the evidence. Retention periods are set by law and contract; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Q. What is a related-party transaction?

A. A deal between parties connected by ownership, family or control, which needs disclosure and an independent check because the usual tension between buyer and seller is missing.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Ford, with Cole beside me for the audit questions. As an owner you will commission buildings with thousands of products and dozens of consultants, and you will never personally test a cladding panel or read the fire test report for every product on site. You will rely on certificates, test reports and sign-offs. Grenfell shows what happens when everyone relies and no one verifies. The facts here are kept to those widely reported; for detail, read the inquiry reports themselves.

Step 1: Timeline

Grenfell Tower was a residential tower block in London, built in the 1970s. A refurbishment completed in 2016 added new windows and an external cladding system, including aluminium composite panels with a polyethylene core over combustible insulation. On 14 June 2017 a fire that began in a flat spread up the outside of the building and around it. Seventy-two people died. A public inquiry reported on the night itself in 2019 and published its final report on the wider causes in September 2024.

Step 2: Key decisions

The refurbishment chose an external cladding system for appearance, insulation and cost. Products were selected and substituted during design and procurement. Each consultant and contractor relied on product marketing, test results and certificates, and on the building control process, to conclude the system was acceptable. The final report found that the decisive failures were spread across many parties rather than resting on one.

Step 3: Assumptions

The assumptions were familiar. That a product sold for use on tall buildings must be safe for that use. That a certificate described the product as actually supplied and installed. That someone else, the architect, the contractor, the fire engineer or building control, had checked the whole system rather than its parts. That regulatory guidance was clear. The inquiry found each of these unsafe.

Step 4: Incentives

The final report found that some manufacturers had acted dishonestly in how they tested and marketed their products, presenting results in ways that concealed how they behaved in fire. Consultants and contractors worked to cost and programme pressure. Regulators and testing bodies were found to have failed in their own oversight. No party was paid to own the integrated question: how does this whole wall behave in a fire?

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The final report described earlier fires involving combustible cladding, in Britain and abroad, and concerns raised within government and industry over many years that did not lead to effective action. At project level, questions about product combustibility were not pursued to a firm answer. Cole's audit lens: a warning that is noted but assigned to no one is not a control; it is a record that the risk was known.

Cole's audit questions

Cole here. An auditor reading a project after a failure like this asks a short, uncomfortable set of questions, and you can ask them of your own project before anything happens. Who signed off the whole wall, as opposed to its parts? What evidence did they hold, and was it about the product actually delivered to site, or about a product with a similar name? When a product was substituted, who reviewed the change, and is that review in writing? Where is the list of fire-related warnings raised during design and construction, and what happened to each one? Who had the authority to stop the work, and did they know they had it?

If the honest answer to any of these is "everyone" or "I assumed the architect," then on your project nobody owns that question. The inquiry's findings are a public record of what that answer costs. The fix is cheap compared with the risk: one named reviewer, one substitution procedure, one warning log with owners and dates.

Step 6: Point of no return

For the building, the point of no return was installation: once the system was on the wall, the risk was built in, and only removal could take it out. For the people, it was the night of the fire. For an owner, the lesson is that the cheap moment to challenge a product is before it is ordered, and the next cheapest is before it is installed.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause, in plain terms, was assurance without verification. Every party held a piece of paper; nobody held responsibility for testing the paper against the real product in the real system. In the language of this phase, risk was allocated by contract and by certificate but never challenged by an independent reviewer with the authority to stop the work.

What an owner can take from it

Two worked checks, both hypothetical. First, a product substitution. A contractor proposes swapping a specified panel for a cheaper one, saving 200,000 dollars on a 30,000,000-dollar job. The saving is 0.67 percent of the contract. If the substitute changes the fire performance of the wall and requires later removal at, say, 3,000,000 dollars, plus loss of use, the saving is worth nothing. The control is a substitution procedure: no change to a life-safety product without the fire engineer's written review of the whole system, and the test evidence for the product as it will be installed.

Second, a certificate audit. Before acceptance, pick five life-safety products and ask four questions of each certificate: does it describe this exact product, does it cover this use and configuration, is the issuing body independent and recognised, and is the certificate current. On many real projects at least one answer is no, and you want to learn that before the scaffold comes down.

Professional sign-off required: fire protection engineer, on the façade and fire strategy; architect and envelope consultant, on the wall system. The code basis is the American standards your design team adopts, such as the International Building Code and the National Fire Protection Association standards for exterior wall assemblies; verify against the current adopted edition.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that every party on your project believes another party has checked the whole system. The control is to name, in writing, one competent and independent reviewer for each life-safety system, with authority to hold the work.

The beginner's mistake

Accepting a value-engineering saving because the substitute is described as equivalent. Equivalent must be shown with evidence for the product as installed, not asserted in a covering letter.

Callback

In Week 49, the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse of 1981 showed a change that nobody re-checked. Grenfell shows the same failure at the scale of a whole supply chain: a substitution or a system that every party saw in part and no party owned as a whole.

Recap

Grenfell burned in 2017 and the inquiry reported in 2024 on failures across manufacturers, consultants, contractors, regulators and government. The root cause was assurance without verification. Rule 84: verify the paper, especially on life-safety systems.

Next: Priya, on The Money: what transferring risk actually costs, and what keeping it costs.
checklist: Every life-safety system has one named, independent reviewer with authority to hold the work.
No substitution of a life-safety product proceeds without a written system review.
I check that each certificate describes the exact product, use and configuration installed.
I check the issuing body is independent and the certificate is current.
I audit a sample of life-safety certificates before acceptance.
I record every safety warning with a named owner and a closing date.
I treat a value-engineering saving on a safety product as unproven until evidenced.
head: Field checklist
speak: Grenfell Tower in London burned on 14 June 2017 and 72 people died. A refurbishment finished in 2016 had added external cladding, including aluminium composite panels with a polyethylene core over combustible insulation. The public inquiry's final report in September 2024 described failures spread across manufacturers, consultants, contractors, testing bodies, regulators and government, including dishonest testing and marketing by some manufacturers. Almost every party held a document that said the system was acceptable, and no party owned the question of whether the whole wall was safe in a fire. That is assurance without verification. For me as an owner, the rule is that a certificate is a claim to check, not a risk transferred. I name one independent reviewer for each life-safety system, with authority to stop the work, and I let no safety product be substituted without a written review of the whole system.
terms: Assurance — a statement, certificate or report that something meets a standard, which is only as good as the evidence behind it.
Product substitution — replacing a specified product with another during procurement or construction, which must be reviewed for performance as installed.
System performance — how an assembly of products behaves together, which can differ from how each product behaves when tested alone.

hostile.q: Your consultants and the manufacturer have all certified the façade. Why are you paying for another review?
hostile.a: Because certificates describe products and parts, and the risk is in the whole system as installed. I pay one independent reviewer to own the integrated question and to check that each certificate matches the product, use and configuration we actually built. Grenfell showed what happens when every party relies on someone else's paper.

rule: Rule 84: Never accept a certificate, test report or sign-off on a life-safety system as proof until an independent reviewer with authority to stop the work has checked it against the product and the system actually being built.

title: The Price of Moving Risk: Premiums, Bonds, Caps and Contingency
summary: Every risk can be kept, priced into a contract, insured or bonded, and each choice has a cost. This lesson compares those costs on one hypothetical project and shows how they move the budget, the lender's sizing and your return. Moving risk is not free, and keeping it is not free either.
body:
You pay for every risk on a project once, either up front as a premium or a contractor's margin, or later as a loss. The skill is choosing which price to pay, and knowing the number before you choose.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 84?

A. Never accept a certificate or sign-off on a life-safety system as proof until an independent reviewer with authority to stop the work has checked it against the product and system actually being built.

Q. What does privilege protect?

A. Certain confidential communications, mainly with lawyers for legal advice or in contemplation of litigation, from being disclosed. Its scope varies by jurisdiction, and it can be lost by careless sharing.

Q. What is a capital call?

A. A demand that partners contribute more money under the partnership agreement, with consequences, such as dilution, for a partner who does not pay.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, contractors, insurers and sureties are not charities. When they take a risk, they charge for it, and the charge sits in your budget. When you keep a risk, you carry it as contingency, and the contingency sits in your budget too and in the equity the lender makes you hold. Both choices change the cost line, the loan size and the return. This lesson puts numbers on them.

Four ways to hold a risk

In plain English: you can keep a risk, make the contractor take it, insure it, or have someone guarantee it.

Professionally, there are four prices. Retention costs contingency: money in the budget you may not spend, which still has to be funded. Contractual transfer costs margin: a contractor who accepts more risk adds a premium to its price, and a lump sum with heavy risk transfer usually costs more than one with shared risk. Insurance costs premium plus deductible: you pay a known amount for cover of defined events, and you still bear the deductible and anything excluded. Surety costs a bond premium, which the contractor usually passes through to you, for a third party's promise to pay if the contractor defaults. The rates for all of these are commercial practice set by markets, not standards.

Worked example, hypothetical numbers. A 40,000,000-dollar build has a ground risk with an expected cost of 600,000 dollars: a 30 percent chance of a 2,000,000-dollar problem. Option one, keep it: carry contingency. If the lender wants contingency at the severe case, not the expected one, you fund 2,000,000 dollars. Option two, transfer it: the contractor adds 900,000 dollars to its price to accept ground risk, the expected cost plus a margin for its uncertainty. Option three, share it with a baseline report: the contractor adds 300,000 dollars and you keep the worse-than-baseline tail, carrying 1,000,000 dollars of contingency. The expected total cost is close in all three. What differs is how much money sits idle in the budget and who decides when the problem appears.

Say that out loud now.

How the choice moves the lender and the return

In plain English: money you hold back for problems is money you must raise, and raising it costs return.

Professionally, contingency is part of total development cost. Lenders size the loan to a percentage of cost or value, and the gap is your equity. Suppose the lender lends 60 percent of cost. In option one, total cost carries 2,000,000 dollars of contingency, so 800,000 dollars of it is equity. In option two, the 900,000-dollar premium is cost too, so 360,000 dollars is equity, but it is spent, not held. In option three, the 300,000-dollar premium plus 1,000,000 dollars of contingency gives 520,000 dollars of equity.

Now the return. Unspent contingency usually comes back to you at completion, so holding it costs you the time value of that equity, not the money itself. A premium paid to a contractor never comes back. If the problem never appears, option one returns the full 2,000,000 dollars and looks best. If the problem appears in full, option two looks best, because someone else paid. A sponsor who chooses by the expected value alone ignores the thing a lender cares about most: what happens in the severe case.

A deductible is a retained risk in disguise

In plain English: every time something goes wrong, you pay the first slice yourself.

Professionally, a deductible applies per event, unless the policy says otherwise, so a project with many small events can retain more than one with a single large one. Worked example, hypothetical. A builder's risk policy has a deductible of 250,000 dollars per event. Over a two-year build you suffer three water events of 150,000 dollars each and one storm loss of 1,200,000 dollars. The three small events fall entirely inside the deductible: 450,000 dollars retained, nothing recovered. The storm recovers 1,200,000 minus 250,000, which is 950,000 dollars, before any exclusion. Total retained: 450,000 plus 250,000, or 700,000 dollars. If your register carried insurance as if it removed water risk entirely, it under-priced the retained portion by 700,000 dollars. A lower deductible costs a higher premium; the choice is a trade between a known cost now and a retained cost later, and it belongs in the register as a retained risk, not as cover.

Bonds and letters of credit are priced differently

A performance bond, typically a percentage of the contract sum, gives you a surety to call on if the contractor defaults; the surety may complete the work or pay up to the bond amount, and the process can be slow and contested. A letter of credit from the contractor's bank is usually paid on demand against documents, which is faster and more certain, and so it costs the contractor more and ties up its banking lines. On a hypothetical 40,000,000-dollar contract, a bond of 10 percent gives you 4,000,000 dollars of cover against the cost of replacing a failed contractor. If replacing it would cost 6,000,000 dollars in premium to a new contractor and delay, the bond covers two thirds, and the rest belongs in your register.

Design risk has its own price

Professional indemnity insurance covers a consultant's liability for negligent design or advice, up to the policy limit, usually on a claims-made basis, meaning the policy in force when the claim is made responds, not the one in force when the design was done. For an owner, that means two checks. First, the limit: a design error that costs 5,000,000 dollars to fix is only partly covered by a consultant carrying a 2,000,000-dollar limit, and the consultant's own assets may not cover the rest. Second, continuity: the consultant must keep the cover in place for years after completion, because defects surface late. Ask for the limit in the appointment and for evidence of renewal each year. The premium is the consultant's cost, but it appears in the consultant's fee, so it is part of your soft costs too.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet: every risk the project keeps is ultimately backed by your equity, and through any guarantee, by you. Before you choose retention to save a premium, ask what a severe case does to your own liquidity, because a contingency that runs out becomes a capital call on you. A premium is a known small loss; an uninsured severe case is an unknown large one. Choose with your personal liquidity floor in view.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing the cheapest-looking option on expected value and discovering the severe case is unfunded. The control is to show every risk choice in three columns, expected, severe and who pays in the severe case, before deciding.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the insurance premium as the cost of cover and forgetting the deductible, the exclusions and the cost of the claim process. A policy with a deductible of 250,000 dollars per event does not cover the first 250,000 dollars of any event.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught the in-balance test: undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the cost to complete. Every retained risk that happens shows up there. If you chose retention and under-funded the contingency, the out-of-balance notice is where you find out, and the deposit comes from you.

Recap

Keep, transfer, insure or bond: each has a price. Contingency is held and usually returns; premiums are spent. Lenders size against total cost, so both change your equity. Compare choices on the severe case, not only the expected one.

Next: Vera, on The Rules: notices, time bars and the records that decide who carries the loss.
checklist: I show every major risk choice in expected, severe and who-pays-in-severe columns.
I know how my lender treats contingency in the loan sizing.
I know the deductible and the main exclusions on each policy.
I compare a bond's cover with my real cost of replacing a contractor.
I know whether my security is a bond or an on-demand letter of credit.
I check my personal liquidity floor against the severe case before choosing retention.
I record the reason for each keep-or-transfer choice in my decision journal.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every risk on a project is paid for once, either up front or later as a loss. There are four ways to hold it. Keep it, and carry contingency that has to be funded. Transfer it to the contractor, and pay its premium in the price. Insure it, and pay a premium plus the deductible and anything excluded. Bond it, and pay for a surety's promise if the contractor fails. On expected cost the options often look alike. What differs is the severe case and who pays when it happens. Lenders size the loan against total cost, so both contingency and premiums change my equity, but unspent contingency usually comes back and a premium never does. So I show every major choice in three columns: expected, severe, and who pays in the severe case. And because a retained risk is backed by my equity and possibly my guarantee, I check my own liquidity floor before I choose to keep it.
terms: Retention — keeping a risk yourself and carrying contingency against it.
Deductible — the part of each insured loss that the policyholder bears before the insurer pays.
Letter of credit — a bank's undertaking to pay a named party on presentation of specified documents, usually faster and more certain than a bond.

hostile.q: Why are you paying a 900,000-dollar premium for the contractor to take ground risk when the expected cost is only 600,000?
hostile.a: Because the severe case is 2,000,000 dollars, and if I keep it, the lender will require me to fund contingency at that level, which raises my equity and my exposure. The extra 300,000 buys certainty in the case that would otherwise fall on my equity and my guarantee. I have compared all three options on the severe case, and this is the one I can survive.

title: Notices, Time Bars and Proof: The Rules That Decide Who Carries the Loss
summary: Many losses on a project are decided not by who was at fault but by who gave the right notice, on time, with the right evidence. This lesson revisits notice clauses, conditions precedent, time bars, limitation periods, privilege and retention as one system of proof.
body:
On paper, the contract allocates risk. In practice, the party who gave proper notice on time, and can prove it, often keeps the right the contract gave them. The party who did not can lose it entirely.

Recall

Q. What are the four ways to hold a project risk?

A. Keep it with contingency, transfer it to the contractor through the price, insure it, or have it bonded or secured by a third party.

Q. What is the purpose of a dispute board?

A. A standing panel, often appointed at the start of a project, that hears disagreements as they arise and gives decisions or recommendations quickly, so small disputes do not grow while the work continues.

Q. What is drag-along?

A. A right allowing majority holders who sell to require minority holders to sell on the same terms, so a buyer can acquire the whole company.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Vera. Over this phase you met clauses that decide rights and the records that prove facts. Checkpoint week is the moment to see them as one machine. Owners lose recoverable money more often through missed notices and missing evidence than through bad contracts. Think of this lesson as the rulebook for the last two links in LEX's chain, proof and resolution. The rules below are concepts; the exact requirements live in your contract and in the law that governs it, and you must verify each against the primary source before you rely on it.

Notice as a condition precedent

In plain English: some contracts say that if you do not tell the other side about a problem in a set way, within a set time, you lose the right to claim for it.

Professionally, a notice clause is a requirement to inform the other party of an event or claim. When it is drafted as a condition precedent, giving the notice is a condition that must be met before the right to relief exists. When it also has a deadline, it operates as a time bar: miss the deadline and the claim may be barred, however strong it is. Standard forms such as AIA, ConsensusDocs and FIDIC each contain notice requirements, and the FIDIC forms are well known for strict claim notice periods. Whether a time bar is enforced as written depends on the governing law and the facts; courts in different systems take different views, and that is why your lawyer must advise.

Worked example, hypothetical. Your contract requires the contractor to notify a delay event within a set number of days of becoming aware of it, as a condition precedent to an extension of time. A design change on day 30 causes delay; the contractor gives notice on day 90. If the clause is enforced as written, the contractor may lose its extension, and you may be entitled to liquidated damages, here 10,000 dollars a day, for the period. Now reverse it. The same contract requires you, the owner, to notify defects or counter-claims within a set period, and your team forgets. The same rule now strips your claim. A notice clause cuts both ways, so you need a notice calendar for your own obligations as well as theirs.

Say that out loud now.

Limitation periods sit above the contract

In plain English: even with no contract deadline, the law gives you only so long to start a claim.

A limitation period is the time, set by law, within which a claim must be brought in court or arbitration. It usually runs from when the cause of action arose or was discovered, and different claims can have different periods. Latent defects, faults hidden at completion, raise hard questions about when time starts. Do not rely on any number you have heard; limitation periods differ between jurisdictions and between types of claim, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. The practical rule is to diarise the outside date for every potential claim at practical completion and at every defect discovery.

Proof: the record and its protection

In plain English: if you cannot prove it happened, you may as well not have the right.

Three rules govern proof. First, contemporaneous records carry weight: site diaries, dated photographs, minutes, instructions and correspondence made at the time. Second, privilege can protect confidential legal advice and documents prepared for litigation from disclosure, but it can be lost by forwarding advice widely or mixing it with business documents. Third, retention: documents must be kept for as long as claims and legal duties may run, and destroying documents once a dispute is foreseeable can carry serious consequences. Retention periods depend on law and contract; verify them.

Second worked example, hypothetical. A claim for 1,500,000 dollars of disruption rests on the contractor's daily records showing which crews were idle and why. The owner's monitor kept its own diary, which records instructions given and crews on site on the same days. Where the two diaries agree, the facts are settled cheaply. Where they disagree, the one made at the time, signed and unaltered wins credibility. An owner with no diary of its own argues against the contractor's evidence with nothing but memory. The cost of a daily owner's diary over a 24-month build is small; its value in a single dispute can be most of the claim.

The dispute ladder runs on the record

The dispute ladder from Week 81 climbs from site-level negotiation to senior executives, then to a dispute board or adjudication, then mediation, and finally arbitration or court. Each rung costs more time and money than the last, and at each rung the record does most of the work. A dispute board decides quickly on the documents in front of it. A mediator helps parties see the strength of each other's evidence. An arbitrator or judge decides on evidence tested by cross-examination. The party with clear notices and contemporaneous records can often settle on a lower rung, because the other side can see how the higher rungs would end. Many contracts also make the lower rungs a condition precedent to the higher ones, so a party who skips a step may find its arbitration paused until it goes back. Read the dispute clause as part of the notice calendar, because its steps have deadlines too.

The governance of notices

Every notice clause names an address and often a form. Decide who in your company may issue and receive notices, where they are logged, and who reviews the log weekly. A notice sent to an old address, by the wrong method, or signed by someone without authority can be challenged. Treat the notice log like the draw certificate: a document with legal effect, owned by a named person.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on notice clauses, time bars, limitation and privilege under the governing law.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a valid claim lost to a missed deadline. The control is a notice calendar with every contractual and legal deadline, owned by one person, checked weekly, and triggered by the event log rather than by memory.

The beginner's mistake

Raising a problem in a site meeting and assuming that counts as notice. Minutes may help as evidence, but most contracts require notice in a specified form to a specified address. Say it in the meeting, then send the notice.

Callback

In Week 35, Omar and LEX taught signing authority and minute books. A notice is a corporate act, just like signing a loan. The same discipline applies: decide in writing who may do it, record it when done, and keep the evidence where it can be found years later.

Recap

Notice clauses, often conditions precedent with time bars, decide whether rights survive. Limitation periods set an outside date in law. Contemporaneous records, protected privilege and proper retention decide whether you can prove anything. Keep a notice calendar for both sides.

Next: Roman, on The Numbers: reverse engineering a settled dispute back to the contingency that should have covered it.
checklist: I keep a notice calendar covering my obligations and the contractor's.
One named person owns the notice log and reviews it weekly.
I know which notice clauses are conditions precedent or time bars.
I diarise the outside limitation date for each potential claim at completion.
My monitor or site team keeps a signed, dated daily diary.
Legal advice is kept separate from business files and shared only on a need-to-know basis.
I know the notice address, method and authorised signatory for every contract.
head: Field checklist
speak: Owners lose recoverable money more often through missed notices and missing evidence than through bad contracts. Many contracts make notice a condition precedent: if you do not tell the other side in the right form and within the deadline, you may lose the right, however good the claim. That cuts both ways, so I keep a notice calendar for my own obligations as well as the contractor's. Above the contract sits the limitation period, the time the law gives to start a claim. I never rely on a number I have heard; I verify it for the jurisdiction and claim type, and I diarise the outside date at completion. Then there is proof. Contemporaneous records, signed and dated, carry weight. Privileged advice must stay separate or the protection can be lost. And documents must be kept as long as claims can run. A notice is a corporate act, so one named person owns the log.
terms: Condition precedent — a requirement that must be satisfied before a right, such as an extension of time, comes into existence.
Time bar — a deadline after which a claim is lost if notice or action has not been taken.
Limitation period — the time set by law within which a claim must be started in court or arbitration.

hostile.q: Your project manager raised the delay in three site meetings. Why do you say you may have lost the claim?
hostile.a: Because our contract makes written notice to a specified address within a set period a condition precedent, and minutes of a meeting may not satisfy it. Whether the bar is enforced as written depends on the governing law and the facts, and our lawyer is advising. From today the notice log is owned by one person and checked weekly, so it cannot happen again.

title: Reverse Engineering a Settled Claim: From the Final Account Back to the Risk Register
summary: Start with a finished project whose final account was 4,000,000 dollars over budget after a settled dispute, and work backward. Split the overrun into what the contract allocated, what insurance and bonds paid, what the register should have carried and what the missing records cost. Every dollar traces to one link in the chain.
body:
An overrun is not one number. Taken apart, it shows which link in the risk chain broke: the allocation, the backstop, the register, the dispute or the record. Each link has its own fix.

Recall

Q. What is a time bar?

A. A deadline after which a claim is lost if the required notice or action has not been taken.

Q. What does a Monte Carlo analysis do for contingency?

A. It runs the cost or schedule model thousands of times with each risk drawn from its range, giving a distribution of outcomes, so contingency can be set at a chosen confidence level rather than as a flat percentage.

Q. What does misrepresentation mean in an offering document?

A. A false or misleading statement of fact, or a material omission, that an investor relied on, which can give rise to liability.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Roman. This is an even week, so we work backward from a finished outcome. Lenders and investors do exactly this after a bad project: they take the final number and ask where it came from. If you can do it to your own hypothetical project first, you will design the next one so the chain does not break in the same place. All figures below are hypothetical round numbers.

The finished outcome

A hypothetical 50,000,000-dollar project, including a 2,000,000-dollar contingency, finished with a final account of 56,000,000 dollars. The project was 6,000,000 dollars over its budget excluding contingency, and 4,000,000 dollars over after the contingency was consumed. The owner funded the 4,000,000 dollars with new equity. Our job is to explain the 6,000,000 dollars of gross overrun, link by link.

Step 1: Separate the events

The cost report lists three events. Event A, unforeseen ground: 2,500,000 dollars. Event B, a subcontractor insolvency on the façade: 2,000,000 dollars. Event C, a delay dispute settled at 1,500,000 dollars paid to the contractor. Check: 2,500,000 plus 2,000,000 plus 1,500,000 is 6,000,000 dollars. The pieces add up, so we can trace each one.

Step 2: Event A against the allocation link

The contract used a baseline geotechnical report. The contractor carried conditions up to the baseline; the owner carried conditions worse than it. The actual ground was worse, so the owner paid 2,500,000 dollars. Was this a failure? Look at the register. It carried ground risk at an expected value of 500,000 dollars and no severe case. The allocation worked exactly as written; the register under-priced the owner's share. Lesson: the register must hold the owner's side of every shared risk at its severe value, here something near the full 2,500,000 dollars.

There is a second check here. Was the owner's payment of 2,500,000 dollars actually due? Under a baseline report, the contractor must prove the conditions were worse than the baseline, quantity by quantity. The site records show the rock was surveyed jointly when exposed and the volumes agreed in writing. That record is why this event settled without a dispute. Had the volumes not been agreed at the time, the owner would have paid an estimate rather than a measured quantity. On this project the record link held for Event A, and its strength is visible in how cheaply it closed.

Step 3: Event B against the backstop link

The façade subcontractor failed. The main contractor carried that risk under the contract, but the main contractor claimed the failure arose from an owner-nominated subcontractor, so it sought relief. The owner had nominated the firm to save time. A performance bond from the subcontractor existed at 10 percent of its 8,000,000-dollar package, so 800,000 dollars, and the surety paid 600,000 dollars after negotiation. Net cost to the owner: 2,000,000 minus 600,000 is 1,400,000 dollars. The rest of the 2,000,000 dollars, the 600,000 recovered, was covered. So of Event B, 1,400,000 dollars stuck. Lesson: nominating a subcontractor can pull its risk back to the owner, and a bond sized at 10 percent rarely covers the true cost of replacement.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3a: Check the ledger against the events

The gross 6,000,000 dollars counts Event B at its full 2,000,000. But the surety paid 600,000 dollars, so the true net overrun is 6,000,000 minus 600,000, which is 5,400,000 dollars. After the 2,000,000-dollar contingency, the owner's new equity should have been 3,400,000 dollars, not 4,000,000. Why the difference? The surety's payment arrived after the final account was closed and was banked to the company's general account, never credited back to the project. The project's books therefore overstate the overrun by 600,000 dollars, and the investors were told a worse number than the truth. Lesson: a reverse engineer checks the ledger as well as the events, and every recovery is traced to the line it belongs to.

Step 4: Event C against the record link

The delay dispute settled at 1,500,000 dollars. The contractor claimed 2,500,000 dollars of prolongation, a cost for each extra day on site. The owner believed some of the delay was the contractor's own and some was concurrent. But the owner kept no daily diary of its own, and its monitor's reports were monthly summaries. In mediation, the owner could challenge the contractor's records only with recollection. The owner's lawyer estimated that with a contemporaneous owner's diary, the settlement might have been nearer 800,000 dollars. That is an estimate, not a fact, but the gap, about 700,000 dollars, is the price of a missing record.

Step 5: Rebuild the ledger

LinkEventNet cost, dollarsAvoidable or under-priced
RegisterA, ground worse than baseline2,500,000under-priced by 2,000,000
BackstopB, nominated subcontractor1,400,000largely avoidable
RecordC, delay settlement1,500,000about 700,000
Total5,400,000

Read the table as a lender would. The contingency of 2,000,000 dollars was not too small for a risk profile like this one; it was mis-aimed. A register priced at severe values on the owner's own shared risks would have shown about 4,500,000 dollars needed: the 2,500,000 ground tail plus a 2,000,000 allowance for contractor-chain default. That is the number the owner should have held, or reduced by better allocation.

Step 5a: What a Monte Carlo would have said

Run the register again with honest ranges. Ground worse than baseline: a 40 percent chance, cost between 1,000,000 and 3,000,000 dollars. Contractor-chain default: a 20 percent chance, net cost between 1,000,000 and 2,500,000 after bonds. Delay claim exposure: a 50 percent chance, between 500,000 and 2,000,000 dollars. Thousands of simulated projects drawn from those ranges give a distribution. A typical result for inputs like these would put the median total near 2,000,000 dollars and the 90th percentile well above 4,000,000. The original 2,000,000-dollar contingency sat near the middle: a coin flip. The lender, who wanted protection at a high confidence level, would have asked for a number near the 90th percentile. These ranges are illustrative; your quantity surveyor builds the real ones from your project.

Step 6: The prevention plan

For the next project: price the owner's side of every shared risk at its severe value; never nominate a subcontractor without writing down whose risk its failure becomes; size bonds against real replacement cost; keep an owner's daily diary from the first day on site; and reconcile recoveries to the line they belong to.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating the overrun as bad luck and repeating the structure. The control is this reverse engineer, done within a month of the final account and written into your decision journal.

The beginner's mistake

Accepting the gross overrun figure without checking recoveries. Here the owner over-funded by 600,000 dollars because a surety payment sat on the wrong line.

Callback

In Week 51, Quincy taught cost-to-complete and earned value. A reverse engineer is the same discipline after the fact: every dollar mapped to a line, every line to a cause, and the forecast compared with what actually happened.

Recap

A hypothetical 6,000,000-dollar gross overrun became 5,400,000 net after a recovery, and traced to three links: an under-priced register, a nominated subcontractor and a missing record. Each has a fix you can write into the next project.

Next: Cole, on The Room: a mock meeting with the lender's monitor, the insurer's adjuster and the contractor in one room.
checklist: I reverse engineer every final account within a month of receiving it.
I split every overrun into events and check that the events add up.
I check recoveries are booked against the line they belong to.
My register prices the owner's side of every shared risk at its severe value.
I write down whose risk a nominated subcontractor's failure becomes.
I size bonds against the real cost of replacement, not a habit percentage.
I record the findings and the prevention plan in my decision journal.
head: Field checklist
speak: An overrun is not one number. Take a hypothetical 50,000,000-dollar project with a 2,000,000-dollar contingency that came in 6,000,000 dollars over before contingency. Split it into events: ground worse than the baseline report, 2,500,000; a nominated façade subcontractor that failed, 2,000,000; and a delay settlement, 1,500,000. Then check the ledger: a surety paid 600,000 dollars that was booked on the wrong line, so the true net overrun was 5,400,000. Now trace each event to a link. The ground risk was allocated correctly but the register priced the owner's share at its expected value, not its severe value. The nominated subcontractor pulled its risk back to the owner, and the bond covered only part of it. The delay settlement was high partly because the owner kept no daily diary. The contingency was not just small; it was aimed at the wrong things. Each link gets its own fix for the next project.
terms: Final account — the agreed total of all sums payable under a construction contract at its end, including variations and settled claims.
Prolongation cost — the time-related cost a contractor incurs for each extra day on site, such as supervision and site facilities.
Nominated subcontractor — a subcontractor chosen by the owner, which can shift the risk of its failure back toward the owner.

hostile.q: Your contingency was 2,000,000 dollars and you needed 5,400,000. Why should I believe your next contingency?
hostile.a: Because I have traced every dollar of the overrun to a cause. The contingency was mis-aimed rather than only small: the register priced our share of ground risk at its expected value and ignored the severe case, and we nominated a subcontractor whose failure came back to us. The next register prices the owner's side of every shared risk at its severe value, and I will show you the line-by-line comparison.

title: Mock Meeting: The Monitor, the Adjuster and the Contractor in One Room
summary: A full mock meeting for the phase. A façade failure has caused water damage and delay; the lender's monitor, the insurer's loss adjuster and the contractor's commercial director all attend. Each reads the same facts for a different purpose. Your job is to keep the claim, the cover and the loan intact at once.
body:
When something goes wrong, every party in the room is protecting its own position with the same set of facts. The owner who has the record, the notice and the allocation ready keeps all three positions intact; the owner who improvises gives one away to win another.

Recall

Q. In the reverse engineer, why was the owner's contingency described as mis-aimed?

A. Because the register priced the owner's share of a shared risk at its expected value instead of its severe value, and missed the risk that a nominated subcontractor's failure would come back to the owner.

Q. What is consequential loss?

A. Indirect loss flowing from a breach or event, such as lost profit or lost rent, as opposed to the direct cost of repair. Many contracts exclude it, and what counts as consequential depends on the wording and the governing law.

Q. What is the question behind a lender asking for a monthly report?

A. Whether you will tell them bad news early or only when they find it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Cole. Checkpoint week ends the room work with a full mock meeting that uses every tool in the phase. You will not often face these three people at once, but you will face them in the same fortnight, and what you say to one becomes evidence for the others. One consistent, evidenced account is the only safe position.

The setup

This is a composite scene with hypothetical facts. Month 18 of a 24-month build. A section of curtain wall failed in a storm; water entered three floors, damaging finished drywall and electrical work. Repair estimate: 1,200,000 dollars direct. The contractor says the storm exceeded design conditions and claims an extension of 60 days. The builder's risk policy has a deductible of 250,000 dollars per event and excludes the cost of correcting defective workmanship, while typically covering resulting damage; the policy words decide. The loan's in-balance margin is 400,000 dollars. In the room: Dana, the lender's monitor; Hal, the insurer's loss adjuster; and Pierce, the contractor's commercial director.

Before the meeting

Three things on the table, prepared in advance. The notice log, showing that you notified the insurer and the contractor in writing within the policy and contract periods. The owner's daily diary and dated photographs from the storm and the days after. A one-page split of the loss into the cost to replace the failed wall components, the resulting damage to other work, and delay. Each person in the room cares about a different line, and you want them to see you know which.

The lines to say

Open with the bottom line: "The direct loss is 1,200,000 dollars and up to 60 days. Here is our split, our notices and our records. My aim today is to agree the facts, not the allocation."

To Hal, the adjuster: "We notified on the day after the storm. This sheet separates the cost of the failed panels from the resulting damage to drywall and electrical work. We understand the policy distinguishes them, and we would like your view on the split in writing."

To Pierce: "We have recorded your 60-day claim. Our contract requires particulars within a set period, and we will assess it on the particulars. In the meantime we need a recovery programme by Friday."

To Dana: "Our worst case is the full 1,200,000 dollars less the deductible not recovered, plus delay. That exceeds our in-balance margin of 400,000 dollars, so we have prepared an equity deposit plan, which I will confirm by Friday."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say to the adjuster, "The contractor clearly installed it wrong." That may be true, and it may also push the whole loss into the defective-workmanship exclusion. Let the evidence speak, and let the engineer give the cause. Never say to the contractor, "Don't worry about the time, we'll sort it out." That can be read as a waiver of the notice requirements. Never say to the monitor, "Insurance will cover it." You do not yet know what insurance will cover, and the monitor will remember the sentence. Never speculate about the cause in front of all three.

The question behind the question

When Hal asks, "Was the wall inspected before the storm?", the question behind it is whether the loss arose from a defect the owner knew about, which may affect cover. Answer with records: "The inspection and test plan for that section shows a water test on these dates, with these results." When Pierce says, "This was a once-in-50-years storm," the question behind it is whether you will accept force majeure without evidence. Answer: "Send us the weather data and the design criteria, and our engineer will compare them." When Dana asks, "When will you know?", the question behind it is whether you have a plan or a hope. Give a date.

When to stay silent

After you state the deposit plan to Dana, stop. After Hal asks for documents, write the list down and say only, "You will have them by Wednesday." When Pierce and Hal begin to argue about the cause, let them; you learn more listening than steering, and you avoid becoming the one who named a cause.

Holding your state

Three parties, a loss that could cost you personally, and an argument in progress. Keep your voice low and slow, put your palms flat on the table, and speak only from the papers in front of you. If you feel the urge to fill a silence, look down at the notice log instead. The meeting does not need to end in agreement; it needs to end with facts agreed, documents listed and dates set.

How the meeting should end

A short summary in writing, sent the same day: facts agreed, facts disputed, documents each party will provide, and dates. Send the same summary to all three, with any privileged legal analysis kept out of it. Then update the risk register and the notice calendar before you go home.

The second meeting

Two weeks later, the engineer's report finds the panel fixings were installed outside the manufacturer's tolerance on one elevation, and the storm was within design conditions. Now the allocation conversation begins, and it is shorter because the facts were agreed first. The contractor's extension claim weakens, since the storm was not exceptional. The adjuster's position on the split between defective components and resulting damage is now a matter of policy words applied to agreed facts. The monitor already holds your equity deposit plan. Your lines in this second meeting stay the same in shape: "Here is the engineer's report. Here is our position under the contract and the policy, from our lawyer. Here is what we need from each of you, and by when." You have not had to retract anything from the first meeting, because you said nothing in it that you could not prove. That is the reward for discipline in the first room.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is saying something to one party that damages your position with another, such as naming the cause in front of the insurer. The control is to prepare one account, stick to the evidence, and let qualified engineers state causes in writing.

The beginner's mistake

Trying to settle allocation in the first meeting. The first meeting agrees facts and dates. Allocation comes later, on the record, through the contract and the policy.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught acknowledge, bridge, answer, and "I'll confirm by Friday." Today you used both: you acknowledged each party's concern, bridged to the evidence, answered with records, and made dated commitments rather than guesses.

Recap

Prepare the notices, the records and a split of the loss before the room. Agree facts, not allocation. Never name a cause in front of the insurer, never waive notice by reassurance, and never promise the lender insurance money you do not have. Summarise in writing the same day.

Next: Kema, on the Checkpoint for contracts, insurance, risk and audit: the mock interview, the recording and the rules.
checklist: I bring the notice log, the daily diary and a split of the loss to any loss meeting.
I agree facts and dates first and leave allocation for later.
I never name a cause of loss in front of an insurer before an engineer has reported.
I never reassure a contractor in a way that could waive a notice requirement.
I never promise a lender insurance proceeds before cover is confirmed.
I send one written summary to all parties the same day, with privileged analysis kept out.
I update the register and the notice calendar after the meeting.
head: Field checklist
speak: A storm breaks a section of curtain wall at month 18, and water damages three floors. The lender's monitor, the insurer's adjuster and the contractor's commercial director all come to one meeting. Each reads the same facts for a different purpose: the adjuster for cover, the contractor for time and money, the monitor for whether the loan stays in balance. I prepare three things: the notice log, the owner's daily diary and photographs, and a one-page split of the loss into failed components, resulting damage and delay. I open with the bottom line and say my aim is to agree facts, not allocation. I never name a cause in front of the insurer, I never reassure the contractor in a way that waives notice, and I never promise the lender insurance money. I give dates instead of hopes. The same day I send one written summary to everyone, and I update the register and the notice calendar.
terms: Loss adjuster — a specialist appointed by an insurer to investigate a claim, establish the facts and assess the amount payable under the policy.
Resulting damage — damage to other work caused by a defect or failure, which some policies cover even when correcting the defect itself is excluded.
Waiver — giving up a right, which can sometimes be inferred from words or conduct, such as reassuring a party that a deadline does not matter.

hostile.q: Your contractor caused this failure. Why should the policy pay anything?
hostile.a: I am not stating the cause; our engineer will report on that in writing. What I can show you today is that we notified on time, that our records cover the inspection, testing and the storm, and a split of the loss between the failed components and the resulting damage to other work. I would like your view on that split under the policy words, in writing.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Checkpoint: Contracts, Insurance, Risk and Audit
summary: This is the checkpoint for the contracts, insurance, risk and audit phase. Answer six mock interview questions aloud, record a three-minute explanation on your phone, score it from 1 to 5 on accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, and then read every rule so far aloud and restate it.
body:
A phase is learned when you can explain it under pressure, out loud, without notes. Today you test whether you can walk a lender or partner through how risk on a project is allocated, funded, owned, proved and challenged, and you write down the score.

Recall

Q. In the mock meeting, what should you never say in front of the loss adjuster?

A. A cause of the loss, such as "the contractor installed it wrong," before an engineer has reported, because it may push the loss into an exclusion.

Q. What does Rule 84 say?

A. Never accept a certificate or sign-off on a life-safety system as proof until an independent reviewer with authority to stop the work has checked it against the product and system actually built.

Q. What is the outside view, or reference class forecasting?

A. Judging a project by how similar projects actually turned out, rather than by the details of your own plan alone.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Kema. Every other phase taught you how to make money on a project. This one taught you how to keep it when something goes wrong. Recognition comes from reading; performance comes from saying it aloud under pressure. This checkpoint measures performance and gives you a score to beat next time.

The mock interview

Imagine a senior lender's credit officer across the table. Read each question, answer aloud before reading the model answer, and be strict with yourself.

Question 1. Your contract allocates ground risk to the contractor. Is the risk gone?

Answer: No. Allocation is only as good as the backstop. The residual, the contractor's insolvency, a dispute over the clause or a claim that the ground was unforeseeable, stays with me, and I carry contingency sized to the contractor's balance sheet and security.

Question 2. What does a liquidated damages clause do to your delay risk?

Answer: It prices a slice of it. I recover a fixed daily rate up to a cap. If my own daily cost of delay is higher, or the delay runs past the cap, the rest is mine. I know the day the cap is reached and carry it in my downside case.

Question 3. Why might a policy not pay for a failed façade?

Answer: Because of the deductible, exclusions such as the cost of correcting defective workmanship, late notice, or a dispute about cause. The policy words decide, not the broker's summary, so I read the exclusions and notify on time.

Question 4. How can a strong claim be lost?

Answer: By missing a notice that is a condition precedent, by a time bar, by a limitation period, or by having no contemporaneous record to prove it. A notice calendar for both sides and a daily owner's diary are the controls.

Question 5. How do you size contingency?

Answer: From a risk register with an owner, trigger and range for each risk, priced at a chosen confidence level, often with Monte Carlo analysis, and with the owner's side of every shared risk held at its severe value.

Question 6. Why pay for independent review when your consultants have certified everything?

Answer: Because assurance is not verification. A reviewer with no stake in the decisions, and authority to stop the work, tests the paper against the real product and system. Grenfell, in 2017, showed what reliance without verification can cost. Rule 84.

Say that out loud now.

The recorded explanation

Now the real test. Open the voice recorder on your phone and record a three-minute explanation of this phase, as if to a new equity partner who asks, "If something goes badly wrong on site, who pays, and how do we know?" Use this order: the six links, allocation, transfer, retention, resolution, proof and challenge; one worked example with hypothetical numbers, such as a liquidated damages cap; how insurance and bonds back the allocation and what they leave out; how notices and records keep rights alive; and one failure case with its rule. No notes. Do not restart if you stumble; stumbling is data.

Listen back once and score yourself from 1 to 5 on each of four measures:

  1. Accuracy. Were the definitions and numbers right? A 5 has no errors; a 3 has one material slip, such as saying a liquidated damages clause removes delay risk.
  2. Structure. Did you lead with the bottom line and follow the order? A 5 could be written down as an outline.
  3. Composure. Was the pace steady, with pauses instead of filler? A 5 sounds like someone who has done this many times.
  4. The hard question. Did you name, unprompted, the risk that is still yours after every allocation and policy? A 5 raises it before the listener can.

Write the four scores and the date in your decision journal. An example of honest scoring: if you said "the contractor carries that risk" without mentioning the contractor's ability to pay, accuracy is a 2, because the phase's central idea is that a clause allocates but does not pay.

What to do with the scores

Act on your lowest score alone this week. If accuracy was lowest, reread the lesson the error came from and restate the definition in your own words. If structure was lowest, write the six links on a card and record again from the card. If composure was lowest, record again more slowly and count filler words. If the hard question was lowest, practise opening with "What is still ours after all of this is..." until it comes first by habit. Record again at the end of the week and compare.

A model outline for the recording

One: "Every risk ends up with somebody, and we choose who in writing before the loss." Two: "Six links: the contract allocates, insurance and bonds fund, the register owns the rest, the dispute ladder settles the unclear, records prove, independent review tests." Three: "A liquidated damages cap of 2,000,000 dollars is reached at day 200; every day after is ours." Four: "Policies have deductibles and exclusions, and notices keep rights alive." Five: "What is still ours is contractor default and the severe side of shared risks, and we fund it." Six: "Rule 84." That runs about three minutes at a steady pace.

How this phase joins the others

Notice how much of this phase leaned on earlier ones. The risk register is the stress test from the capital phase, aimed at specific events. The insurance programme is part of the lender's security from construction lending. The records are the same evidence discipline that keeps a cross-border structure defensible. When you record today, try to say one sentence that links risk allocation back to the lender: every risk the owner keeps is ultimately funded by equity, and the lender sizes that equity.

Rules I will not break

Below this lesson is the list of rules you have committed to so far, one from each failure case, now including Rule 84. Read each rule below aloud, then restate it in your own words. If you cannot restate a rule without looking, mark it and reread the lesson it came from this week.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk at a checkpoint is grading what you meant instead of what you said. The recording does not know what you meant. Score the tape.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the model answers instead of recording. Reading feels like mastery and proves nothing; hearing yourself explain risk under pressure is the rehearsal that makes the real meeting familiar.

Callback

In Week 65, the cross-border checkpoint asked you to defend a structure chart. Listen for whether today's recording connects the two: an entity structure and a risk allocation are both promises you must be able to prove with records, and both fail where nobody owns the evidence.

Recap

Answer the six questions aloud. Record three minutes on who pays when things go wrong, score accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question from 1 to 5, and write the scores in your journal. Read every rule aloud and restate it.

checklist: RULES_SO_FAR
head: Rules I will not break
speak: Every risk on a project ends up with somebody, and the work is to choose that somebody in writing before the loss arrives. The contract allocates the risk. Insurance and bonds put money behind it, but every policy has deductibles and exclusions, and every bond has a limit. The risk register owns what is left, with the owner's side of every shared risk priced at its severe value. The dispute ladder settles what the paper left unclear, and notices, time bars and limitation periods decide whether rights survive long enough to be argued. Contemporaneous records prove what happened. Independent review tests whether the rest is real, because assurance is not verification, which is what Grenfell showed in 2017. So when a partner asks who pays if something goes badly wrong, my answer starts with what is still ours after every clause and policy, how much it is, and how we have funded it.
terms: Checkpoint — a scheduled test of whether a phase can be explained aloud under pressure, scored and recorded.
Decision journal — a dated written record of decisions, the reasons for them and the expected outcome, reviewed later against what happened.
Residual risk — the part of a risk that remains with you after allocation, insurance and security have done their work.

hostile.q: After all these contracts, policies and bonds, what risk is still yours?
hostile.a: Three things. Contractor and subcontractor default beyond the bond amounts; the severe side of shared risks, such as ground worse than the baseline report; and anything excluded or below the deductible in the policies. I have priced each in the register at its severe value, and the contingency and my equity plan are sized to cover them.
